transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you in today?

Well, the biggest thing—the thing that finally made me come in—is my sleep. It’s gotten completely unmoored, I guess is the word. At first it was almost strange because I’d sleep maybe two or three hours and then I’d be up, wide awake, making plans, writing things down, feeling like I was ready to go and didn’t really need more rest.

But now it’s not like that in any useful way. I’m lying awake before dawn, just staring or turning things over in my head, and my stomach is tight, like I’m bracing for something. Even if I’ve technically been in bed, I don’t feel rested. It feels like my body has forgotten how to sleep properly. That’s what brought me in.
Have there been times when you felt unusually energetic, maybe even like you didn’t need much sleep, where your thoughts were racing or you were doing a lot of things at once—maybe more than usual?

Yes—yes, that’s exactly part of what has been happening. It’s hard to describe without sounding like I’m exaggerating, but it felt like there was an engine running inside me. Like I couldn’t just sit quietly with a cup of coffee or read the paper like a normal morning. I’d be up before sunrise, already making calls or thinking of who I needed to call, and then I’d be rewriting proposals—things that probably didn’t need rewriting right then—and jumping from one thing to the next.

I wasn’t finishing one task in a steady way, either. It was more like I’d start something, then another idea would grab me, and I’d move to that, and then suddenly I’d remember some other plan and be halfway into that. Sitting still felt almost impossible, like I was wasting time if I wasn’t doing something. At the time it felt productive, or at least urgent, but looking back it was… a lot. More than usual for me, definitely.
After those periods of high energy and being very active, did you experience a time when you felt down most of the day, lost interest in things you usually enjoy, or had other symptoms of depression?

Yes. Afterward, it was like everything just… went flat. Not just tired, exactly, though I suppose tired is part of it. More like the color went out of things I normally care about.

I used to be able to spend whole afternoons at the museum, just wandering from room to room and noticing little details in paintings, or I’d take my camera out and lose track of time photographing light on buildings, reflections, people’s hands, all sorts of ordinary things. And cooking, too—I used to enjoy the whole process, planning a meal, chopping, getting the timing right. Even bridge, which I’ve played for years, usually gives me something to look forward to.

But lately I look at the camera sitting there, or think about going to the museum, or see the bridge table, and I just feel… nothing. Or not nothing exactly—more like I can immediately feel the effort it would take to pretend I was enjoying it. Like I’d have to act interested, act like myself. And that feels exhausting before I’ve even started.

Can you think of a time when your mood was unusually high, elated, or irritable for several days in a row, along with more energy than usual—like you didn’t need much sleep and had a lot of things going on in your mind?

Yes. There was a stretch—longer than just a few good days, really, it went on for weeks—where I felt almost… brilliantly optimistic, I suppose. Like everything was suddenly obvious to me, and every problem that had seemed complicated before was actually quite manageable, almost trivial. I remember thinking, why has everyone been making such heavy weather of things? It all felt so clear.

And I had much more energy with it. I didn’t experience it as “too much” at the time, though. I thought I was finally operating at the level I was supposed to be operating at. I’d have all these things going on in my mind at once, and they didn’t feel disorganized to me then—they felt important, connected, urgent.

But the other side of it was that I got very sharp with people. If someone questioned me, even gently, I took it very badly. I’d snap at them, as if they were deliberately getting in the way or trying to undermine me. In my head it was like, I’m the only person seeing this clearly, and everyone else is slowing me down. Looking back, that sounds awful, but at the time I really did feel like I was the only sensible man in the room.
